sourceTitle: How Do We Keep an Eye on Asteroids?
scoreRule: 1 point per correct MC item; 10 points maximum; local provisional grade only
description: EN/B1 independently drafted Asteroids Reading test; not reviewed by second teacher.

tabs.title: Understanding the message
tabs.description: Interpret the passage and its purpose.

tabs.title: Reasons and connections
tabs.description: Find explanations supported by the text.

tabs.title: Use what you have read
tabs.description: Apply the information to new situations.

questions.q: Why might scientists be interested in an asteroid that is not dangerous to Earth?
choices: It may soon become a planet.
It can provide clues about how the early solar system developed.
It may be visible from every city at night.
It will certainly pass close to Earth next year.
questions.explanation: The first paragraph says asteroid materials and shapes provide evidence about the distant past.

questions.q: What does the writer suggest about an early orbit prediction?
choices: It should be shared only after it becomes certain.
It is usually accurate enough after one photograph.
It is likely to be wrong because asteroids have no regular paths.
It may need adjustment when astronomers obtain more observations.
questions.explanation: Recently discovered objects have uncertain orbit estimates that improve with repeated measurements.

questions.q: Why is the DART event described as a controlled test rather than a rescue?
choices: The spacecraft was unable to reach the small asteroid.
It was launched after an asteroid had already hit Earth.
The chosen object was not a real threat to our planet.
Scientists did not measure the effects of the impact.
questions.explanation: DART intentionally struck a safe target to prepare for a possible future problem.

questions.q: What was the most important danger to people in Chelyabinsk?
choices: Broken windows sent pieces of glass flying.
The impact made a very large crater.
The rock caused a fire throughout the city.
The asteroid blocked sunlight for several hours.
questions.explanation: The shock wave broke windows and many injuries were caused by flying glass.

questions.q: Why is international cooperation useful when tracking a newly found object?
choices: Scientists can change its composition by sharing pictures.
Shared measurements can improve an estimate of where it is going.
Different observatories can make it stop moving.
Scientists can avoid checking predictions with computers.
questions.explanation: The article explains that researchers cooperate and share observations to refine orbits.

questions.q: Why was the Chelyabinsk object especially hard to spot before it arrived?
choices: It had no solid parts for telescopes to detect.
It moved more slowly than a normal asteroid.
It came from a direction hidden by bright sunlight.
It spent many years hidden behind Jupiter.
questions.explanation: Bright sunlight in the arrival direction made detection difficult.

questions.q: Why would an early warning matter even if a spacecraft could change an asteroid's orbit?
choices: An early warning is useful only after a collision.
Spacecraft are unable to alter any asteroid's movement.
Scientists would not need to calculate the orbit.
A response takes time to plan and observations help people decide.
questions.explanation: The conclusion joins early information with any later technical response.

questions.q: A news story says a newly detected object is a 'near-Earth asteroid'. What should a reader conclude?
choices: It is confirmed to be on a collision course.
Its orbit comes into Earth's neighbourhood, but impact is not certain.
The object is already inside Earth's atmosphere.
A spacecraft must be sent to it at once.
questions.explanation: The writer defines near-Earth as orbital proximity rather than a prediction of impact.

questions.q: A classmate becomes frightened by a headline about an asteroid passing near us. Which response fits the writer's advice?
choices: Look for accurate measurements and ask what the report really means.
Assume every close approach can cause a catastrophe.
Ignore all reports because large impacts are rare.
Believe the headline without reading the details.
questions.explanation: Good explanations and careful observations prevent unnecessary panic about close approaches.

questions.q: What is a fair conclusion from a successful experiment like DART?
choices: The next asteroid danger can always be prevented.
All objects in space behave in exactly the same way.
The experiment proves that the sky no longer needs monitoring.
A tested technique may help in the future but still needs preparation.
questions.explanation: The experiment demonstrates a possible intervention, but a future threat would require early detection and decisions.
